title: Virtual Machines vs Containers ⚖️
description: Compare traditional virtualisation with containerisation and see the key differences.

slides.title: Traditional Virtual Machines 🖥️
slides.content:
# How VMs Work

A hypervisor sits on top of the physical hardware and creates multiple **virtual machines**. Each VM:

- Has its own **full operating system** (guest OS).
- Requires a fixed amount of RAM, CPU and disk.
- Starts slowly (minutes) because the guest OS must boot.

## Pros & Cons

✅ Strong isolation – each VM is a complete sandbox.
❌ Heavy resource usage – running many VMs quickly exhausts the host.

slides.title: Container Architecture 🐳
slides.content:
# How Containers Work

Containers run directly on the **host OS kernel**. They don’t need a hypervisor or a guest OS.

- Multiple containers share the same kernel.
- Each container has its own filesystem, processes, network stack, etc.
- They start almost instantly (like a normal process).

## Pros & Cons

✅ Extremely lightweight and fast.
✅ Higher density – run hundreds of containers on a single server.
⚠ Slightly weaker isolation than VMs (but still very secure with modern features).

quizData.question: Why can you run many more containers than virtual machines on the same hardware?

options.text: Containers use a hypervisor that compresses memory.
Containers share the host OS kernel and don’t require a full guest OS.
Containers automatically scale down when idle.

quizData.explanation: Because containers share the host’s OS kernel, they avoid the overhead of running multiple full operating systems. This frees up RAM, CPU and disk.

slides.title: Resource Comparison (Illustrative) 🧮
slides.content: The following snippet shows how you might compare resource usage (conceptual):
slides.codeSnippet:
# Typical VM: 
# OS overhead ~ 1-2 GB RAM per VM
# Boot time ~ 30-120 seconds

# Docker container:
# Overhead negligible (a few MB)
# Start time < 1 second

slides.title: Important Clarification ⚠️
slides.content:
## Containers are NOT mini‑VMs

- They do not virtualise hardware.
- They are **application‑level** isolation powered by Linux features like **namespaces** and **cgroups**.
- On Windows and macOS, Docker runs a lightweight Linux VM to provide the Linux kernel (this is hidden from you).
